claims.text: The untreated alloy is equiatomic NbMoTaW.
Untreated equiatomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC alloy.
Untreated NbMoTaW has very poor room-temperature ductility.
Untreated NbMoTaW has excellent high-temperature strength, including at 1600 °C.
NbMoTaW has theoretically predicted irradiation resistance.
Warm rolling at 800–900 °C followed by a short anneal near 1100 °C can produce a refined, partially recrystallized NbMoTaW microstructure.
The proposed thermomechanical treatment will create stable subgrain boundaries in NbMoTaW.
The refined microstructure reduces barriers to dislocation motion at room temperature.
Reduced barriers to room-temperature dislocation motion enhance NbMoTaW ductility and strain accommodation.
Stable subgrain boundaries act as sinks for irradiation-induced defects.
Stable subgrain boundaries retard dislocation creep and thereby preserve high-temperature strength.
The processed alloy will have significantly greater room-temperature elongation than untreated NbMoTaW.
The processed alloy will retain mechanical strength and creep resistance comparable to untreated NbMoTaW at 1600 °C.
The processed alloy will retain irradiation resistance comparable to untreated NbMoTaW, as assessed through defect evolution and hardness retention.
An inert processing atmosphere is needed to avoid oxidation.
Excessive processing can cause grain coarsening or secondary-phase formation that compromises high-temperature properties.
The intervention may not extrapolate to non-equiatomic or multiphase alloy systems.
Room-temperature tensile testing, 1600 °C mechanical testing, and ion-irradiation testing against an untreated control can jointly evaluate the predicted trade-offs.
Three-MeV Fe-ion irradiation with measurements of dislocation loops and hardness changes is an applicable irradiation assessment protocol.
